text: George Alexander Trebek (/trəˈbɛk/; July 22, 1940 – November 8, 2020) was a Canadian and American game show host and television personality, regarded as a pop culture icon. He is best known for hosting the syndicated quiz show Jeopardy! for 37 seasons from its revival in 1984 until his death in 2020. Trebek also hosted several other game shows, including The Wizard of Odds, Double Dare, High Rollers, Battlestars, Classic Concentration, and To Tell the Truth. He made appearances, usually as himself, in numerous films and television series. Born in Greater Sudbury, Ontario, Canada, on July 22, 1940, Trebek is the son of George Edward Trebek (born Terebeychuk, Ukrainian: Теребейчу́к), a chef who emigrated from Ukraine as a child and spent formative years in Japan, and Lucille Marie Lagacé (April 14, 1921 – 2016), a Franco-Ontarian. His second nickname, Sai, originated from his father's time in Japan. Trebek had roots in Renfrew County, Ontario, where his maternal grandmother was born in Mount St. Patrick near Renfrew. He grew up in a bilingual French-English household and was almost expelled from boarding school; he attended a military college in Quebec but dropped out when asked to shave his head. His first job at age 13 was as a bellhop at the hotel where his father worked. He attended Sudbury High School (now Sudbury Secondary School) and the University of Ottawa, graduating in 1961 with a degree in philosophy. While a student, he was a member of the English Debating Society and was interested in a broadcast news career. Before completing his degree, he began working for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in 1961, reading the national radio news and covering events such as curling and horse racing. His first hosting job was on the Canadian music program Music Hop in 1963, followed by hosting a high school quiz show, Reach for the Top, in 1966. From 1967 to 1970, he hosted CBC classical music programs featuring Glenn Gould and hosted a weekly skating program for one or two seasons. Starting April 1, 1969, he hosted Strategy, a weekday afternoon game show. From 1971 to the end of 1972, he hosted I'm Here Til 9, a local morning drive radio show on CBC Toronto. In 1971, he was shortlisted to succeed Ward Cornell as host of Hockey Night in Canada, though executive producer Ralph Mellanby chose Dave Hodge instead, citing a preference against a host with a mustache. In 1973, Trebek moved to the United States and hosted The Wizard of Odds for NBC. The following year, he hosted High Rollers, which aired on NBC in two incarnations (1974–76 and 1978–80) and a syndicated season (1975–76). Between High Rollers stints, he hosted the short-lived CBS game show Double Dare (not to be confused with the 1986 Nickelodeon show of the same name), which was his only CBS game show hosting role (he returned in 1994 to host the Pillsbury Bake-Off until 1998), and the second season of the syndicated The $128,000 Question, recorded in Toronto. Since the second High Rollers incarnation premiered while The $128,000 Question was still airing, Trebek became one of two hosts to emcee shows in both the U.S. and Canada, joining Jim Perry. In 1978, Trebek's francophone side was showcased in a special bilingual edition of Reach for the Top and its Radio-Canada counterpart, Génies en herbe, where he alternated between French and English. He made guest appearances as a panelist or player on other shows, including a special week of NBC's Card Sharks in 1980, and won a 3-week charity round-robin tournament against Allen Ludden, Bill Cullen, Wink Martindale, Jack Clark, Tom Kennedy, Gene Rayburn, and Jim Lange, defeating Cullen in the finals. He also appeared as a celebrity teammate on The Magnificent Marble Machine (1975) and To Say the Least (1978), both produced by Merrill Heatter-Bob Quigley Productions. He was a contestant on Celebrity Bowling in 1976, teaming with Jim McKrell and winning against Dick Gautier and Scatman Crothers. After High Rollers ended in 1980, Trebek hosted Battlestars for NBC, which debuted in October 1981 and was cancelled in April 1982 after six months. In September 1981, he took over as host of the syndicated Pitfall, which taped in Vancouver and required him to commute, similar to his earlier roles. Pitfall was cancelled after Catalena Productions went bankrupt, and Trebek was never paid. After both shows ended, he hosted a revival of Battlestars called The New Battlestars, which lasted 13 weeks, and produced pilots for Merrill Heatter and Merv Griffin. For Heatter, he produced Malcolm (an NBC pilot with an animated co-host) and Lucky Numbers, a failed High Rollers revival. For Griffin, who was encouraged to hire Trebek by Lucille Ball, he produced two pilots for a Jeopardy! revival when original host Art Fleming declined due to creative differences. This revival sold, and Trebek began hosting Jeopardy! in 1984 and remained host until his death in 2020. His final episode was scheduled for Christmas Day 2020; however, Sony postponed it to January 4–8, 2021, due to production delays and holiday pre-emptions. Following his death, guest hosts filled in for the remainder of season 37. On July 27, 2022, it was announced that Mayim Bialik and Ken Jennings would become the permanent hosts after Mike Richards, the then-executive producer, was let go following controversy. In 1987, while hosting Jeopardy!, Trebek returned to daytime television as host of NBC's Classic Concentration, his second show for Mark Goodson. He hosted both shows simultaneously until September 20, 1991, when Classic Concentration aired its final first-run episode (NBC aired repeats until 1993). On February 4, 1991, Trebek made broadcast history by becoming the first person to host three American game shows at the same time when he took over from Lynn Swann as host of NBC's To Tell the Truth for Goodson-Todman, hosting it until May 31, 1991. In 1994, Trebek returned to CBS for the first time since hosting Double Dare to host the Pillsbury Bake-Off until 1998. On April Fools' Day 1997, he traded places with Pat Sajak, who hosted Jeopardy! and Trebek hosted Wheel of Fortune with Sajak's wife, Lesly, as co-host. Sajak and Vanna White played contestants at the wheel, with winnings going to charities. Trebek appeared on Celebrity Poker Showdown in 2005 and finished second, losing to Cheryl Hines. On June 24, 2018, he returned as a panelist on the ABC revival of To Tell the Truth. In January 2020, he hosted a primetime special titled The Greatest of All Time on ABC, pitting Brad Rutter, Ken Jennings, and James Holzhauer against each other. He made guest appearances on shows such as Jimmy Kimmel Live! (2008 and 2011) and The Colbert Report series finale. In August 1995, he filled in for Charles Gibson on Good Morning America for a week. He appeared as one of two "Men in Black" in the X-Files episode "Jose Chung's From Outer Space," which aired on April 12, 1996. On June 13, 2014, Guinness World Records recognized Trebek with the record for most episodes of a game show hosted, totaling 6,829 at the time. He also appeared in multiple television commercials. On October 1, 2018, he moderated the only debate in the Pennsylvania governor's race between Democrat Tom Wolf and Republican Scott Wagner. He wanted a more conversational format, dominated the debate by speaking for 41% of it, often discussing himself without allowing candidates to address policy issues, and later apologized, calling himself "naive" and "misunderstood," and expressing sincere apologies to the people of Pennsylvania. In a 2020 ABC special, Trebek was interviewed by Michael Strahan about Jeopardy! and his career. On October 6, 2020, he made a cameo at the 2020 NHL Entry Draft, announcing the Ottawa Senators' third-overall pick, Tim Stützle, in Jeopardy! style. Trebek married broadcaster Elaine Callei in 1974; they had no children but adopted her daughter Nicky, and divorced in 1981. In 1990, he married Jean Currivan, a real estate project manager from New York, with whom he had two children, Matthew and Emily. In 1996, he ran the Olympic torch in Jacksonville, Florida, during its journey to Atlanta. He became a naturalized American citizen in 1998. On January 30, 2004, he escaped serious injury after falling asleep while driving alone on a rural road in Templeton, California, causing his truck to sideswipe mailboxes, fly 45 feet (14 meters) over an embankment, and come to rest against a utility pole. He was not cited and returned to work four days later. Trebek owned and managed a 700-acre (280 ha) ranch near Paso Robles, California, known as Creston Farms, where he bred and trained thoroughbred racehorses. His colt, Reba's Gold, is the stakes-winning son of Slew o' Gold. He sold the operation in 2008, and the property is now Windfall Farms. In a 2018 Vulture interview, Trebek described himself as a political moderate and registered independent with some libertarian leanings and stated he believed in God as a Christian, having been raised Catholic during his childhood and adolescence. He was a longtime philanthropist and activist, active with charities including World Vision Canada, the United Service Organizations, and the United Negro College Fund. He traveled to developing countries with World Vision, taping reports on their work. In 1995, he and the Jeopardy! crew appeared on military bases worldwide to find contestants and boost troop morale. He initially joined the UNCF in the 1980s because of his appearance—due to his afro, mustache, and dark tan—leading to confusion with Black men, and was invited to participate in telethons. In 1998, he donated 74 acres (30 ha) of open land in the Hollywood Hills to the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy. He was awarded one of the American Foundation for the Blind's six yearly Access Awards for his role in accommodating Jeopardy! champion Eddie Timanus. He hosted the annual The Great Canadian Geography Challenge in Canada and the National Geographic Bee in the United States for 25 years, stepping down in 2013. He also served on the advisory board of U.S. English, supporting English as the official language of the United States. In 2016, Trebek donated $5 million to the University of Ottawa to fund the Alex Trebek Forum for Dialogue, which aims to expose students to diverse views through speeches, panels, and lectures. His total contributions to the university at the time reached $7.5 million, funding the Distinguished Speaker Series, which included a presentation by Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee, introduced by Trebek. In 2017, he funded the Alex Trebek Leadership Award at the University of Ottawa, an annual $10,000 award to a summa cum laude graduate demonstrating community leadership. By October 2020, his contributions to the University of Ottawa totaled around $7.5 million.

Alex Trebek hosted the National Geographic Bee in the United States for 25 years, stepping down in 2013, and served on the advisory board of U.S. English, an organization that supports making English the official language of the United States. In 2016, he donated $5 million to the University of Ottawa to fund the Alex Trebek Forum for Dialogue, which aims to expose students to diverse views through speeches, public panels, events, and lectures by University of Ottawa researchers, senior government officials, and international guests. His total contributions to the university by October 2020 had reached approximately $10 million, including a $7.5 million gift that also funded the Distinguished Speaker Series, which featured a presentation by Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee introduced by Trebek. In 2017, he funded the Alex Trebek Leadership Award, an annual $10,000 award given to a summa cum laude graduate who has demonstrated community leadership. In March 2020, Trebek donated $100,000 to Hope of the Valley Rescue Mission in Los Angeles, which replaced the Skateland skating rink and was subsequently named the Trebek Center. Trebek owned a personal wardrobe consisting of dozens of outfits and hundreds of neckties, which his son Matthew donated to The Doe Fund in February 2021, in accordance with a statement Trebek made on his last day of taping. On December 10, 2007, Trebek experienced a minor heart attack at home but returned to work in January 2008. On July 26, 2011, he injured his Achilles tendon while chasing a burglar in his San Francisco hotel room, requiring six weeks in a cast. He had a mild heart attack on June 23, 2012, but returned to work the following month. On December 15, 2017, after a fall in October, he was admitted to Cedars-Sinai Medical Center with a subdural hematoma, underwent surgery to remove blood clots the next day, and was announced as suffering from the fall by Jeopardy!'s verified Twitter account on January 4, 2018; he required a short medical leave and returned to regular hosting in mid-January 2018. In 2018, while interviewed by Harvey Levin on Fox News, Trebek suggested retirement, stating the odds of leaving Jeopardy! in 2020 were 50/50 and a little less, and that he might continue if not making too many mistakes, making an intelligent decision about when to step down. In October 2018, he signed a new contract to host through 2022, stating in January 2019 that although he was beginning to slow down due to age and the show’s 46 taping sessions per year, the schedule remained manageable. On March 6, 2019, at age 78, Trebek announced a stage IV pancreatic cancer diagnosis, having experienced a persistent stomach ache prior to it; in a prepared video, he noted a poor prognosis but committed to aggressively fighting the disease and continuing to host, joking that his contract required him to do so for three more years. Two months later, he reported responding exceptionally well to treatment, with some tumors shrinking to half their size, and credited fans' prayers for the positive results, planning further chemotherapy. He completed that chemotherapy round in time to resume taping in August 2019. Follow-up immunotherapy was ineffective, and he resumed chemotherapy in September. On October 4, 2019, in an interview with Lisa LaFlamme, Trebek said he was not afraid of dying, stating he had lived a full life and was nearing its end, and noted that mouth sores from chemotherapy were interfering with his ability to speak, adding that fans and producers would eventually no longer be able to say, "It's okay." In a December 2019 ABC News interview, he said he would begin exploring experimental treatments and chemotherapies, and despite severe pain and depression, remained in good enough physical condition to handle construction projects. He had already prepared an on-air farewell statement before his diagnosis. In March 2020, Trebek announced he had survived one year of cancer treatment (noting an 18% one-year survival rate), and despite a 7% survival rate for another year, he was confident he would survive, saying ending treatment would be a betrayal to his family, supporters, and to God, along with the many prayers for him. As a precaution, Jeopardy! initially taped episodes without a studio audience due to the COVID-19 pandemic, as Trebek was particularly at risk due to his age and condition; production was later suspended. The show resumed taping in August, in time for the season 37 premiere. On July 16, 2020, Trebek said he still felt fatigued but that chemotherapy was "paying off" and was looking forward to taping again. Five days later, he published his memoir, The Answer Is...: Reflections on My Life. Trebek underwent surgery related to his cancer treatment in October, returned to the show two weeks later, but due to post-surgery pain, had to split his usual five-episode taping session over two days, with those five episodes being his final ones. He taped his last episode on October 29, 2020, just 10 days before his death. On November 8, Ken Jennings substituted as host for Trebek, initially as a temporary replacement after the surgery. Trebek died at his home in Los Angeles at age 80 on November 8, 2020, after 20 months fighting pancreatic cancer, the same illness that affected Jeopardy!'s original host, Art Fleming, who died over 25 years earlier. His death became major global headlines, prompting some of the Big Three networks to break programming for special coverage in the United States. His remains were cremated, and his ashes were given to his wife. His estate was liquidated in an April 2022 estate sale as his daughter prepared to sell his home in Studio City. Shortly after his death, Jeopardy! contestant and future host Ken Jennings, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, and Wheel of Fortune hosts Pat Sajak and Vanna White paid tribute. On the November 9, 2020, episode of Jeopardy!, executive producer Mike Richards opened the show with a statement honoring Trebek, noting the loss to staff, family, and fans, and stating that Trebek taped his final episodes less than two weeks prior. The lights dimmed blue in remembrance, and after each posthumous episode in season 37, a screen read, "Dedicated to Alex Trebek. Forever in our hearts. Always our inspiration." On the first anniversary of his death, which coincided with the first episode Ken Jennings hosted in season 38, a title card read, "Alex Trebek, July 22, 1940 – November 8, 2020. You are missed every day." On the second anniversary, Trebek was honored in a category titled "Remembering Alex Trebek" during the Jeopardy! Round of the 2022 Tournament of Champions special exhibition episode. Various networks aired tributes, including MeTV (playing "What Is... Cliff Clavin?" and "Mama on Jeopardy!"), Buzzr (airing episodes of shows Trebek guest-starred in or hosted), and Game Show Network (airing a Jeopardy! marathon). On the premiere of the rebooted American version of The Chase, host Sara Haines paid tribute at the start of the show. Trebek's final episode aired on January 8, 2021, concluding with a 90-second tribute. On August 19, 2021, the Jeopardy! stage was renamed "The Alex Trebek Stage" with his family present. The United States Postal Service honored Trebek with a commemorative stamp on July 22, 2024, on what would have been his 84th birthday, marking both the 60th anniversary of the Jeopardy! franchise and his naturalized American citizenship. In 1997, Trebek received an honorary Doctor of the University (D.Univ) degree from the University of Ottawa. He received a star on Canada's Walk of Fame in Toronto, eight Outstanding Game Show Host Emmy Awards (1989, 1990, 2003, 2006, 2008, 2019, 2020, and 2021), and a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame at 6501 Hollywood Boulevard. On November 4, 2010, he received the Royal Canadian Geographical Society's gold medal for contributions to geographic education, with previous recipients including Wade Davis (2009), Peter Gzowski (1997), and Mary May Simon (1998). In 2016, he was named Honorary President of the Royal Canadian Geographical Society and attended the opening of its new headquarters in 2018. In 2011, he was announced as a recipient of the Lifetime Achievement Award at the Daytime Emmy Awards and received an Honorary Doctorate from Fordham University. Since June 13, 2014, he has held the Guinness World Record for "the most game show episodes hosted by the same presenter (same program)" with 6,829 episodes of Jeopardy!, overtaking Bob Barker. On May 4, 2015, the University of Ottawa named its alumni hall in his honor as a benefactor. In May 2016, he was awarded the Key to the City by the City of Ottawa. On June 30, 2017, he was named an Officer of the Order of Canada for his iconic achievements in television and promotion of learning, particularly geographical literacy. On June 28, 2019, he received the 2019 Americanism Award from the Daughters of the American Revolution. On January 7, 2020, Trebek and his wife Jean were awarded the Fordham Founder's Award. In December 2019, he was named winner of the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television's Icon Award for the 8th Canadian Screen Awards, presented in a recorded speech released in January 2021 to coincide with the broadcast of his final episode. In July 2021, the Royal Canadian Geographical Society and the National Geographic Society launched The Trebek Initiative to promote emerging Canadian explorers, scientists, educators, and photographers. In August 2021, artist Kevin Ledo created a mural memorializing Trebek on the outer wall of Sudbury Secondary School, where he had attended high school, as part of the Up Here Festival. On September 29, 2022, Trebek was posthumously inducted into the inaugural class of the Jeopardy! Hall of Fame at the first Jeopardy! Honors event, with his widow Jean accepting the award on his behalf. In November 2023, Jean Trebek, alongside Katie Couric (who guest-hosted in March 2021), launched "The Alex Trebek Fund" in partnership with Stand Up to Cancer to support scientists improving pancreatic cancer screening and treatment. On June 21, 2024, the U.S. Postal Service announced a first-class Forever stamp honoring Trebek, released on July 22, 2024, on what would have been his 84th birthday, with the design in the form of a Jeopardy!-style question.
